title: Ascent - Landing Space Shuttle Orbiter Imagery
description: Space Shuttle orbiter landing imagery from Kennedy Space Center.
keywords: GRC-2023-CM-0249, Documentation, Mission Support, Shuttle, Orbiter, Shuttle Landing, Kennedy Space Center, Engineering Footage, STS-122, Atlantis
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: [ Music ]
[ Background music ]
>> The bulk of the engineering footage required
for any given shuttle mission is taken during launch and ascent.
However, a significant effort is dedicated
to documenting the orbiter landings as well.
What we're going to see is two clips
from the Kennedy Space Center shuttle landing facility,
captured on 35-millimeter film at a hundred frames per second.
These are fixed camera mounts showing the approach
and landing of the orbiter.
Now, our first clip shows Atlantis on final approach,
returning from the STS-122 mission.
It's important to note that space shuttles were designed
to land as gliders, without power,
so they had no opportunity to go around.
As a consequence, the mission commander only had one
opportunity to get the vehicle down on the runway,
so managing altitude and kinetic energy, to account for this,
was absolutely critical for a safe landing.
Now, in final approach, orbiters have often been referred
to as flying bricks.
They come down quite fast.
And just before landing, they nose down 19 degrees and descend
on a glide slope seven times steeper and 20 times faster
than a commercial airliner.
At around 2,000 feet in altitude,
the commander flares the vehicle.
And just 15 seconds prior to touchdown,
the landing gear is deployed.
This camera gives a great overall view of the vehicle
on approach and for the most part is intended
to document the performance
of the landing gear and its deployment.
The analysis teams will look for any debris
that might be liberated, as the gear doors open.
And they'll also look at some of the other things, like sink rate
of the vehicle and orientation on final.
>> On this next camera view, we're actually now looking
at Discovery, not Atlantis,
and Discovery's coming back from STS-131.
Basically, we wanted to pick some of the best-looking clips
for this production, and as a consequence,
they weren't the same mission.
Interestingly enough, these two clips were taken almost two
years apart, but they were nearly at the exact same time
in the morning -- 9:07 and 9:08,
just a minute apart from one another.
The shuttle landing strip is an amazing 15,000 feet long,
so those trees you see in the background are
over three miles away.
Look at the wing tips.
You can see some of the vortices shutting off there
and causing kind of a neat atmospheric distortion.
And you can see the crosswinds pushing the vehicle
around a little bit.
Here you see the smoke from the tires getting caught
up in the wing vortices, causing sort
of a sideways tornado effect.
You can see the actuator speed brake in full deployment there.
There's the drogue chute coming
out to pull the main drag chute out.
You can see some hardware flying across the runway there.
The debris team will have to go out and get that hardware later.
All that has to be accounted for.
And if you look at the drag chute,
it's not fully deployed yet.
You'll see it incrementally deploy here.
They do that so it doesn't rip the chute off right away.
So as the speed of the orbiter decreases, the deployment
of the drag chute increases.
There's one of the service vehicles.
There's actually quite an armada of service vehicles
that chase the orbiter down the runway, as soon as it flies by.
Kind of an interesting fun fact: The debris teams --
Bob, Armando, Scott, the guys from one of the commentaries,
actually drive out and drive in the opposite direction,
down to the other end of the runway,
where they will begin their walkdown by foot
of the entire runway, looking for debris, collecting anything
that doesn't belong there
and may have fallen off the orbiter during landing,
and getting some of that hardware
that was liberated during the chute deployment.
